item.title: Features of Propellers
item.description:
DIAMETER D D D
The diameter of the propeller is the diameter of the circle or disc cut out by the blade tips. Increasing a propeller’s diameter will generally increase its efficiency, but this will be limited by the draught and form of the aft part of the ship.

PITCH P P P
Pitch is defined as the distance the propeller would move forwards in one revolution if it were working in an unyielding fluid. This is similar to how a screw thread progresses into wood as it is turned. In reality, water is not an unyielding fluid, and so the propeller would not progress as far as the pitch.

PITCH RATIO p p p, or face pitch ratio, is the face pitch divided by the diameter. Thus:

p=PD p = \frac{P}{D} p=DP​

THEORETICAL SPEED Vt V_t Vt​ is the distance the propeller would advance in unit time if working in an unyielding fluid. Thus, if the propeller turns at N N N rev/min,

Vt=P×N(m/min) V_t = P \times N \quad \text{(m/min)} Vt​=P×N(m/min)

APPARENT SLIP
As described previously, water is not an unyielding fluid, and so the ship speed V V V will normally be less than the theoretical speed. The difference between the two speeds is known as the apparent slip and is usually expressed as a ratio or percentage of the theoretical speed.

Apparent slip speed=Vt−V(knots) \text{Apparent slip speed} = V_t - V \quad \text{(knots)} Apparent slip speed=Vt​−V(knots)

If the ship speed is measured relative to the surrounding water, i.e. by means of a log line or paddle wheel speedometer, the theoretical speed will invariably exceed the ship speed, giving a positive apparent slip. If however, the ship speed is measured relative to the land, then any movement of water will affect the apparent slip, and should the vessel be travelling in a following current the ship speed may exceed the theoretical speed, resulting in a negative apparent slip.

WAKE
In its passage through the water, the ship sets in motion particles of water in its neighbourhood. This moving water is known as the wake and is important in propeller calculation since the propeller works in wake water. The speed of the ship relative to the wake is termed the speed of advance.

SPEED OF ADVANCE Va V_a Va​
The wake speed is often expressed using:

  • Taylor’s Wake Factor
  • Froude’s Wake Factor

The wake fraction may be obtained approximately from the expression

wt=0.5Cb−0.05 w_t = 0.5 C_b - 0.05 wt​=0.5Cb​−0.05

where Cb C_b Cb​ is the block coefficient.

REAL SLIP OR TRUE SLIP is the difference between the theoretical speed and the speed of advance, expressed as a ratio or percentage of the theoretical speed.

Real slip speed=Vt−Va(knots) \text{Real slip speed} = V_t - V_a \quad \text{(knots)} Real slip speed=Vt​−Va​(knots)

The real slip is always positive and is independent of current.

EXAMPLE
A propeller of 4.5 4.5 4.5 m pitch turns at 120 120 120 rev/min and drives the ship at 15.5 15.5 15.5 knots. If the wake fraction is 0.30 0.30 0.30, calculate the apparent slip and the real slip.

Vt=4.5×120×601852=17.49 knots V_t = \frac{4.5 \times 120 \times 60}{1852} = 17.49 \text{ knots} Vt​=18524.5×120×60​=17.49 knots

Apparent slip:

Vt−VVt=17.49−15.517.49=11.38% \frac{V_t - V}{V_t} = \frac{17.49 - 15.5}{17.49} = 11.38\% Vt​Vt​−V​=17.4917.49−15.5​=11.38%

Wake speed = wake fraction × \times × speed of ship:

wtV=V−Va w_t V = V - V_a wt​V=V−Va​

Therefore:

Va=V(1−wt)=15.5×(1−0.3)=15.5×0.7=10.85 knots V_a = V(1 - w_t) = 15.5 \times (1 - 0.3) = 15.5 \times 0.7 = 10.85 \text{ knots} Va​=V(1−wt​)=15.5×(1−0.3)=15.5×0.7=10.85 knots

Real slip:

Vt−VaVt=17.49−10.8517.49=37.96% \frac{V_t - V_a}{V_t} = \frac{17.49 - 10.85}{17.49} = 37.96\% Vt​Vt​−Va​​=17.4917.49−10.85​=37.96%

The relation between the different speeds may be shown clearly by a line diagram.

PROJECTED AREA Ap A_p Ap​ is the sum of the blade areas projected on to a plane that is perpendicular to the axis of the screw.

DEVELOPED AREA is the actual area of the driving faces

  • a) Clear of the boss AD A_D AD​
  • b) Including the boss area AB A_B AB​

BLADE AREA RATIO BAR \text{BAR} BAR is the developed area excluding boss divided by the area of the circle cut out by the blade tips:

BAR=ADπ4D2 \text{BAR} = \frac{A_D}{\frac{\pi}{4} D^2} BAR=4π​D2AD​​

DISC AREA RATIO DAR \text{DAR} DAR is the developed area including boss divided by the area of the circle cut out by the blade tips:

DAR=ABπ4D2 \text{DAR} = \frac{A_B}{\frac{\pi}{4} D^2} DAR=4π​D2AB​​

Thrust
The thrust exerted by a propeller may be calculated approximately by regarding the propeller as a disc that increases the momentum of the water coming into it. Water is received into the propeller disc at the speed of advance and projected aft at the theoretical speed.

Consider a time interval of 1 second.
Let
A A A = Effective disc area in m2 \mathrm{m}^2 m2 = disc area − boss area
ρ \rho ρ = density of water in kg/m3 \mathrm{kg/m}^3 kg/m3
P P P = pitch of propeller in m \mathrm{m} m
N N N = revs/s
Va V_a Va​ = speed of advance in m/s \mathrm{m/s} m/s

Mass of water passing through disc in 1 second:

M=ρAPNkg M = \rho A P N \quad \text{kg} M=ρAPNkg

Change in velocity:

PN−Vam/s P N - V_a \quad \text{m/s} PN−Va​m/s

Since this change in velocity occurs within 1 second, the acceleration a a a is:

a=PN−Vam/s2 a = P N - V_a \quad \text{m/s}^2 a=PN−Va​m/s2

But real slip s s s is:

PN−Va=s PN P N - V_a = s \, P N PN−Va​=sPNa=s PN a = s \, P N a=sPN

Since Force = mass × \times × acceleration,

Thrust T=M×a=ρAPN×s PN=ρAP2N2sNewton \text{Thrust } T = M \times a = \rho A P N \times s \, P N = \rho A P^2 N^2 s \quad \text{Newton} Thrust T=M×a=ρAPN×sPN=ρAP2N2sNewton

It is interesting to note that increased slip leads to increased thrust and that the propeller will not exert a thrust with zero slip. The power produced by the propeller is known as the thrust power (tp tp tp):

tp=Thrust (N)×speed of advance (m/s)=T×VaW tp = \text{Thrust (N)} \times \text{speed of advance (m/s)} = T \times V_a \quad \text{W} tp=Thrust (N)×speed of advance (m/s)=T×Va​W

item.title: Powering and Resistance
item.description:
1. Ship Drive Train and Power Hierarchy

Power flows from the engine to the hull, experiencing losses at each stage. The relative magnitude follows: BHP>SP>DP>TP>EPBHP > SP > DP > TP > EPBHP>SP>DP>TP>EP

    graph TD
    BHP[Brake Horsepower - Engine Output] -->|Reduction Gear Losses| SP[Shaft Power - After Gears]
    SP -->|Bearing & Seal Losses| DP[Delivered Power - At Propeller]
    DP -->|Propeller Losses| TP[Thrust Power - Generated by Screw]
    TP -->|Hull-Propeller Interaction| EP[Effective Power - Bare Hull Resistance]

Definitions & Key Equations

  • Effective Power (EP): Power required to tow/move the bare ship hull at speed VsV_sVs​ without propeller action. EP=Rt×VsEP = R_t \times V_sEP=Rt​×Vs​

  • Brake Horsepower (BHP): Power output at the engine shaft before reduction gears.

  • Shaft Power (SP): Power output coming out of the reduction gears.

  • Delivered Power (DP): Power delivered directly to the propeller. DP=SP−losses in shafting, bearings, and sealsDP = SP - \text{losses in shafting, bearings, and seals}DP=SP−losses in shafting, bearings, and seals

  • Thrust Power (TP): Power created by the propeller. TP=DP−propeller losses=T×VaTP = DP - \text{propeller losses} = T \times V_aTP=DP−propeller losses=T×Va​

2. Propulsion Efficiencies

Losses along the drive train are quantified using efficiencies (η\etaη):

  • Gear Efficiency: ηgear=SPBHP\eta_{gear} = \frac{SP}{BHP}ηgear​=BHPSP​ (Typical: ∼98−99%\sim 98 - 99\%∼98−99%)

  • Shaft Transmission Efficiency: ηshaft=DPSP\eta_{shaft} = \frac{DP}{SP}ηshaft​=SPDP​ (Typical: ∼97−98%\sim 97 - 98\%∼97−98%)

  • Propeller Efficiency: ηpropeller=TPDP\eta_{propeller} = \frac{TP}{DP}ηpropeller​=DPTP​ (Typical: ∼70−75%\sim 70 - 75\%∼70−75%)

  • Hull Efficiency: ηH=EPTP\eta_{H} = \frac{EP}{TP}ηH​=TPEP​ (Well-designed: ηH>1\eta_H > 1ηH​>1; Poorly-designed: ηH<1\eta_H < 1ηH​<1)

  • Propulsive Coefficient (PC): Overall efficiency combining bearing, guide, and propeller losses. ηp=PC=EPSP\eta_{p} = PC = \frac{EP}{SP}ηp​=PC=SPEP​ (Typical range: 55%−75%55\% - 75\%55%−75%)

3. Total Hull Resistance and Components

Total hull resistance (RtR_tRt​ or RTR_TRT​) is the force opposing ship motion, broken down into three principal components: RT=RAA+RW+RVR_T = R_{AA} + R_W + R_VRT​=RAA​+RW​+RV​

    graph TD
    RT[Total Hull Resistance Rt] --> RAA[Air Resistance R_AA - Superstructure Calm Air]
    RT --> RW[Wave-Making Resistance R_W - Gravity & Speed Dependent]
    RT --> RV[Viscous Resistance R_V - Skin Friction & Form Drag]

Resistance Components & Formulas

  • Air Resistance (RAAR_{AA}RAA​): Caused by airflow over the superstructure (typically 4%−8%4\% - 8\%4%−8% of total resistance).

  • Wave-Making Resistance (RWR_WRW​): Caused by surface waves generated by the moving hull. Affected by beam-to-length ratio, displacement, hull shape, and Froude number.

  • Theoretical wave length: Lwave=2πV2gL_{wave} = \frac{2\pi V^2}{g}Lwave​=g2πV2​

  • Hull speed limit: V=1.34LsV = 1.34 \sqrt{L_s}V=1.34Ls​​ (resistance increases sharply when ship speed approaches hull speed).

  • Viscous Resistance (RVR_VRV​): Combines skin friction and viscous pressure drag.

  • Total Resistance Coefficient: CT=CV+CW+CA=CF(1+K)+CW+CAC_T = C_V + C_W + C_A = C_F(1 + K) + C_W + C_ACT​=CV​+CW​+CA​=CF​(1+K)+CW​+CA​

  • Tangential skin friction coefficient (ITTC 1957 line): CF=0.075(log⁡10Rn−2)2C_F = \frac{0.075}{(\log_{10} R_n - 2)^2}CF​=(log10​Rn​−2)20.075​

  • Reynolds Number: Rn=LVsνR_n = \frac{L V_s}{\nu}Rn​=νLVs​​, where kinematic viscosity ν=1.140×10−6 m2/s\nu = 1.140 \times 10^{-6} \, m^2/sν=1.140×10−6m2/s (fresh water) or 1.190×10−6 m2/s1.190 \times 10^{-6} \, m^2/s1.190×10−6m2/s (salt water).

  • Form Factor (KKK) for normal component multiplier: K=19[∇LBTBL]2K = 19 \left[ \frac{\nabla}{L B T} \frac{B}{L} \right]^2K=19[LBT∇​LB​]2

  • Total Resistance equation: Rt=0.5ρSVs2⋅CTR_t = 0.5 \rho S V_s^2 \cdot C_TRt​=0.5ρSVs2​⋅CT​

  • Correlation Allowance (CAC_ACA​): Accounts for full-scale hull surface roughness, paint texture, and corrosion.

4. Model Testing and Similitude (Froude’s Law)

Because analytical modeling of 3D viscous and wave-making flow is complex, towing tanks use geometrically and dynamically similar models.

  • Scale Factor (λ\lambdaλ): λ=LsLm\lambda = \frac{L_s}{L_m}λ=Lm​Ls​​

  • Area scale: λ2=SsSm\lambda^2 = \frac{S_s}{S_m}λ2=Sm​Ss​​

  • Volume/Displacement scale: λ3=∇s∇m\lambda^3 = \frac{\nabla_s}{\nabla_m}λ3=∇m​∇s​​

  • Law of Corresponding Speeds (Froude Similarity): Dynamic similarity for wave-making requires equal Froude numbers. VsLs=VmLm  ⟹  Vm=Vsλ−1/2\frac{V_s}{\sqrt{L_s}} = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt{L_m}} \implies V_m = V_s \lambda^{-1/2}Ls​​Vs​​=Lm​​Vm​​⟹Vm​=Vs​λ−1/2

5. Screw Propellers and Performance Mechanics

Terminology & Geometry

  • Diameter (DDD): Tip-to-tip circle diameter.

  • Pitch (PPP): Theoretical distance a propeller moves forward in one revolution through an unyielding fluid.

  • Pitch Angle (ϕ\phiϕ): Blade angle relative to incoming flow, calculated as tan⁡ϕ=P2πr\tan \phi = \frac{P}{2\pi r}tanϕ=2πrP​.

  • Speed of Advance (VaV_aVa​): Ship speed accounting for the wake velocity field (VwV_wVw​): Va=Vs(1−Wt)V_a = V_s (1 - W_t)Va​=Vs​(1−Wt​), where WtW_tWt​ is Taylor’s wake fraction (Wt≈0.5Cb−0.05W_t \approx 0.5 C_b - 0.05Wt​≈0.5Cb​−0.05).

  • Slip:

  • Apparent Slip Speed = Vt−VsV_t - V_sVt​−Vs​, where theoretical speed Vt=P×NV_t = P \times NVt​=P×N.

  • Real Slip Speed = Vt−VaV_t - V_aVt​−Va​.

Propeller Forces & Coefficients

  • Thrust Force (TTT): Estimated by momentum change through the propeller disc: T=ρAP2N2sT = \rho A P^2 N^2 sT=ρAP2N2s (where sss is real slip, AAA is effective disc area, NNN is revs/sec).

  • Thrust Coefficient (KTK_TKT​): KT=Tρn2D4K_T = \frac{T}{\rho n^2 D^4}KT​=ρn2D4T​

  • Thrust Loading Coefficient (CtC_tCt​): Ct=T0.5ρVa2AoC_t = \frac{T}{0.5 \rho V_a^2 A_o}Ct​=0.5ρVa2​Ao​T​

  • Ideal Propeller Efficiency: ηpropeller=21+1+Ct\eta_{propeller} = \frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{1 + C_t}}ηpropeller​=1+1+Ct​​2​

Cavitation

  • Definition: Formation and collapse of vapor bubbles when local blade pressure drops below the vapor pressure (PvP_vPv​ of water).

  • Consequences: Loss of propeller efficiency, severe mechanical erosion, noise, and structural vibration.

  • Mitigation: Smooth surfaces (free of fouling/nicks), gradual RPM adjustments, proper pitch control, and increased hydrostatic pressure (e.g., deeper submarine diving depth).

item.title: Resistance and Powering of Ships
item.description:
1. Powering chain

Effective power is the power needed to tow the bare hull at a specified speed, without propeller action.

    flowchart LR
    A[Engine] --> B[BHP]
    B --> C[Reduction gear]
    C --> D[Shaft power SP]
    D --> E[Shafting bearings and seals]
    E --> F[Delivered power DP]
    F --> G[Propeller]
    G --> H[Thrust power TP]
    H --> I[Hull-propeller interaction]
    I --> J[Effective power EP]

The normal relationship is BHP>SP>DP>TP>EPBHP > SP > DP > TP > EPBHP>SP>DP>TP>EP, because power is lost through gears, bearings, seals, propeller action, friction, heat, vibration and sound.

  • Brake horsepower (BHP): Engine output before the reduction gear.
  • Shaft power (SP): Power available after the reduction gear.
  • Delivered power (DP): Power delivered to the propeller.
  • Thrust power (TP): Power generated by propeller thrust.
  • Effective power (EP): Power required to overcome total hull resistance.

2. Power and efficiency formulas

Effective power is

EP=RTVS\mathrm{EP}=R_TV_SEP=RT​VS​

where RTR_TRT​ is total resistance in newtons and VSV_SVS​ is ship speed in metres per second.

The principal efficiencies are:

  • Gear efficiency: ηgear=SPBHP\eta_{\mathrm{gear}}=\frac{SP}{BHP}ηgear​=BHPSP​
  • Shaft transmission efficiency: ηshaft=DPSP\eta_{\mathrm{shaft}}=\frac{DP}{SP}ηshaft​=SPDP​
  • Propeller efficiency: ηprop=TPDP\eta_{\mathrm{prop}}=\frac{TP}{DP}ηprop​=DPTP​
  • Hull efficiency: ηH=EPTP\eta_H=\frac{EP}{TP}ηH​=TPEP​
  • Overall propulsive efficiency: ηP=EPSP\eta_P=\frac{EP}{SP}ηP​=SPEP​

Therefore,

ηP=ηshaftηpropηH\eta_P=\eta_{\mathrm{shaft}}\eta_{\mathrm{prop}}\eta_HηP​=ηshaft​ηprop​ηH​

and

EP=SPηPEP=SP\eta_PEP=SPηP​

Thus, the required shaft power is

SP=EPηPSP=\frac{EP}{\eta_P}SP=ηP​EP​

The overall power relationship is

EP=BHPηgearηshaftηpropηHEP=BHP\eta_{\mathrm{gear}}\eta_{\mathrm{shaft}}\eta_{\mathrm{prop}}\eta_HEP=BHPηgear​ηshaft​ηprop​ηH​

Typical approximate values are:

Efficiency Typical value
Gear efficiency 98%−99%98\%-99\%98%−99%
Shaft efficiency 97%−98%97\%-98\%97%−98%
Propeller efficiency 70%−75%70\%-75\%70%−75%
Overall propulsive efficiency 55%−75%55\%-75\%55%−75%

Example: If EP=23,500 HPEP=23{,}500\ \mathrm{HP}EP=23,500 HP and ηP=0.68\eta_P=0.68ηP​=0.68,

SP=23,5000.68=34,559 HPSP=\frac{23{,}500}{0.68}=34{,}559\ \mathrm{HP}SP=0.6823,500​=34,559 HP

3. Total hull resistance

Total hull resistance is the force opposing ship motion.

The basic resistance components are

RT=RAA+RW+RVR_T=R_{AA}+R_W+R_VRT​=RAA​+RW​+RV​

where:

  • RAAR_{AA}RAA​: Calm-air resistance on the above-water structure.
  • RWR_WRW​: Wave-making resistance.
  • RVR_VRV​: Viscous resistance, including frictional and form resistance.

Additional resistances may include appendage resistance, steering resistance, added resistance in waves and shallow-water resistance.

Main concepts

  • At low speed, viscous resistance generally dominates.
  • At higher speed, wave-making resistance rises rapidly.
  • Air resistance is commonly about 4%−8%4\%-8\%4%−8% of total resistance.
  • Appendage resistance may be significant, especially in naval vessels.
  • Fouling, corrosion and rough paint increase resistance.
  • Shallow water increases flow velocity beneath the hull, pressure changes, wave-making resistance and frictional resistance.

4. Resistance coefficients

The coefficient of total resistance is

CT=RT12ρSVS2C_T=\frac{R_T}{\frac{1}{2}\rho S V_S^2}CT​=21​ρSVS2​RT​​

Therefore,

RT=CT(12ρSVS2)R_T=C_T\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho S V_S^2\right)RT​=CT​(21​ρSVS2​)

where:

  • ρ\rhoρ: Water density.
  • SSS: Wetted surface area.
  • VSV_SVS​: Ship speed.

The total coefficient may be expressed as

CT=CV+CW+CAC_T=C_V+C_W+C_ACT​=CV​+CW​+CA​

or, when correlation allowance is included,

CT=CV+CW+CA+CA,corrC_T=C_V+C_W+C_A+C_{A,\mathrm{corr}}CT​=CV​+CW​+CA​+CA,corr​

where:

  • CVC_VCV​: Viscous-resistance coefficient.
  • CWC_WCW​: Wave-making-resistance coefficient.
  • CAC_ACA​: Air-resistance coefficient.
  • CA,corrC_{A,\mathrm{corr}}CA,corr​: Correlation allowance for full-scale effects.

5. Viscous resistance

Viscous resistance results from water viscosity and pressure changes around the hull.

The viscous coefficient is

CV=CF+KCF=(1+K)CFC_V=C_F+KC_F=(1+K)C_FCV​=CF​+KCF​=(1+K)CF​

where:

  • CFC_FCF​: Skin-friction coefficient.
  • KKK: Form factor.
  • KCFKC_FKCF​: Viscous pressure or form-drag component.

The Reynolds number is

Re=VSLνRe=\frac{V_SL}{\nu}Re=νVS​L​

where LLL is ship length and ν\nuν is kinematic viscosity.

A commonly used ITTC skin-friction relation is

CF=0.075(log⁡10Re−2)2C_F=\frac{0.075}{(\log_{10}Re-2)^2}CF​=(log10​Re−2)20.075​

Approximate flow regimes over a flat plate are:

  • Laminar flow: Re<5×105Re<5\times10^5Re<5×105.
  • Turbulent flow: Re>5×105Re>5\times10^5Re>5×105.

Form factor

A fuller hull generally has a greater form factor and produces more pressure drag. A slender hull reduces pressure differences and eddy formation.

One empirical form-factor expression given in the notes is

K=19(BL)2(TB)0.5(∇L3)0.5K=19\left(\frac{B}{L}\right)^2\left(\frac{T}{B}\right)^{0.5}\left(\frac{\nabla}{L^3}\right)^{0.5}K=19(LB​)2(BT​)0.5(L3∇​)0.5

where BBB is beam, TTT is draft and ∇\nabla∇ is displacement volume.

Boundary-layer separation 

    flowchart LR
    A[Flow along hull] --> B[Boundary layer develops]
    B --> C[Adverse pressure gradient]
    C --> D[Boundary-layer separation]
    D --> E[Wake and eddies]
    E --> F[Viscous pressure/form drag]

Boundary-layer separation causes a large wake and increases pressure drag. It can be reduced by using a slender, smoothly faired hull.

6. Froude number and wave resistance

The Froude number compares inertia forces with gravity forces:

Fn=VSgLFn=\frac{V_S}{\sqrt{gL}}Fn=gL​VS​​

where ggg is gravitational acceleration and LLL is characteristic ship length.

The speed-to-length ratio is

VSL\frac{V_S}{\sqrt{L}}L​VS​​

but it is not dimensionless.

Wave resistance depends mainly on:

  • Froude number.
  • Beam-to-length ratio.
  • Displacement.
  • Hull shape.
  • Ship length and speed.

Ship-generated waves consist mainly of:

  • Transverse waves.
  • Divergent waves from the bow and stern.

The approximate wavelength of the generated wave is

λW=2πVS2g\lambda_W=\frac{2\pi V_S^2}{g}λW​=g2πVS2​​

The approximate hull-speed relationship is

VH=1.34Lft knotsV_H=1.34\sqrt{L_{\mathrm{ft}}}\ \mathrm{knots}VH​=1.34Lft​​ knots

At hull speed, the transverse wavelength becomes approximately equal to ship length. Wave-making resistance then increases sharply.

  • A hump occurs when bow and stern waves reinforce each other.
  • A hollow occurs when they partially cancel each other.
  • Increasing ship length raises hull speed.
  • A bulbous bow can reduce bow-wave resistance through wave interaction.

7. Model testing and scaling

A towing-tank model requires geometric and dynamic similarity.

The scale factor is

λ=LSLM\lambda=\frac{L_S}{L_M}λ=LM​LS​​

where subscripts SSS and MMM denote ship and model.

Scaling relationships are:

  • Length: LS=λLML_S=\lambda L_MLS​=λLM​
  • Area: SS=λ2SMS_S=\lambda^2S_MSS​=λ2SM​
  • Volume or displacement: ∇S=λ3∇M\nabla_S=\lambda^3\nabla_M∇S​=λ3∇M​

For corresponding speeds, Froude’s law gives

VSLS=VMLM\frac{V_S}{\sqrt{L_S}}=\frac{V_M}{\sqrt{L_M}}LS​​VS​​=LM​​VM​​

Therefore,

VM=VSλV_M=\frac{V_S}{\sqrt{\lambda}}VM​=λ​VS​​

and

VS=VMλV_S=V_M\sqrt{\lambda}VS​=VM​λ​

Use SI units for velocity:

1 knot=0.5144 m/s1\ \mathrm{knot}=0.5144\ \mathrm{m/s}1 knot=0.5144 m/s

For dynamically similar testing, the wave-resistance coefficient is transferred as

CW,M=CW,SC_{W,M}=C_{W,S}CW,M​=CW,S​

The model total-resistance coefficient is

CT,M=RT,M12ρMSMVM2C_{T,M}=\frac{R_{T,M}}{\frac{1}{2}\rho_M S_MV_M^2}CT,M​=21​ρM​SM​VM2​RT,M​​

Hence,

CW,M=CT,M−CV,MC_{W,M}=C_{T,M}-C_{V,M}CW,M​=CT,M​−CV,M​

For the full-scale ship,

CT,S=CV,S+CW,S+CA,S+CA,corrC_{T,S}=C_{V,S}+C_{W,S}+C_{A,S}+C_{A,\mathrm{corr}}CT,S​=CV,S​+CW,S​+CA,S​+CA,corr​

Then,

RT,S=CT,S(12ρSSSVS2)R_{T,S}=C_{T,S}\left(\frac{1}{2}\rho_SS_SV_S^2\right)RT,S​=CT,S​(21​ρS​SS​VS2​)

Finally,

EPS=RT,SVSEP_S=R_{T,S}V_SEPS​=RT,S​VS​

8. Propeller terminology 

    flowchart LR
    A[Engine rotation] --> B[Propeller rotation]
    B --> C[Pressure difference over blades]
    C --> D[Water accelerated astern]
    D --> E[Forward thrust]
    E --> F[Ship advances]

Important parts and terms:

  • Diameter DDD: Tip-to-tip distance.
  • Hub: Central connection to the shaft.
  • Blade root: Blade connection to the hub.
  • Blade tip: Outermost part of the blade.
  • Leading edge: First edge to meet incoming flow.

11. Cavitation and ventilation

Cavitation occurs when local pressure on a propeller blade falls below the vapour pressure of water, producing vapour bubbles that subsequently collapse.

Effects include:

  • Reduced propeller efficiency.
  • Loss of thrust.
  • Blade erosion.
  • Vibration.
  • Noise.
  • Possible structural damage.

Cavitation becomes more likely when:

  • Propeller thrust loading is high.
  • RPM changes rapidly.
  • Propeller diameter is too small.
  • Blade surfaces are fouled, nicked or rough.
  • Water pressure is low.

It can be reduced by:

  • Increasing propeller diameter where practicable.
  • Reducing thrust loading.
  • Selecting suitable RPM and pitch.
  • Maintaining smooth, clean blades.
  • Changing RPM gradually.
  • Operating submerged propellers at greater depth when possible.

Ventilation occurs when air or exhaust gas is drawn into a propeller operating close to the free surface. It reduces the water loading on the blades and produces effects similar to cavitation.

12. Practical resistance-reduction measures

  • Keep the underwater hull clean and smooth.
  • Prevent corrosion and marine fouling.
  • Use an efficient, slender hull form.
  • Operate below the resistance-hump speed where practical.
  • Use a properly designed bulbous bow.
  • Optimise propeller diameter, pitch and RPM.
  • Minimise unnecessary appendages.
  • Consider shallow-water effects when selecting operating speed.
